label: Title
notes: Open by shifting attention away from the graph alone and toward the region above the graph. The lecture will reuse the same picture in several forms: a chord test, a Jensen mixture ledger, a domain projection, and a failure check. The point is to make convexity feel testable rather than merely definitional.

label: Epigraph Test
notes: Present the epigraph as the master object. A function value is no longer just a height; it is a lower boundary for all admissible lifted points. If the epigraph is convex, then every segment between two admissible lifted points remains admissible. This gives the chord inequality after choosing boundary points.

label: Chord Inequality
notes: Move from the epigraph to the familiar chord inequality. Choose two boundary points of the epigraph, average them, and read off the vertical coordinate. The graph value at the averaged input must lie no higher than the averaged endpoint values. This is the form students will use in calculations.

label: Domain Convexity
notes: Stress that the domain is not an afterthought. Once convexity is defined through the epigraph, the domain is forced to be convex because it is a linear projection of that epigraph. This also explains why the course allows functions on all of space with plus infinity values: the formula carries its own domain.

label: Jensen Mixing
notes: Treat Jensen's inequality as a bookkeeping device. The table separates the weights, inputs, endpoint values, and weighted endpoint cost. After the inputs are averaged, the function value at the mixed point is much smaller than the weighted endpoint value. The positive residual is a concrete convexity certificate.

label: Affine And Indicator Examples
notes: Use the gallery to connect familiar objects to the same epigraph language. Affine functions are the equality case. Indicator functions encode convex sets by sending points outside the set to plus infinity. Quadratics and smooth functions add differential certificates, where nonnegative curvature gives a local way to certify global chord behavior on convex domains.

label: Maxima And Suprema
notes: Introduce maxima and suprema as upper envelopes rather than as a new theorem to memorize. Each affine function contributes one epigraph half-space, and the intersection remains convex. Support functions fit this template: for each set point, the pairing is affine in the query direction, and the support value takes the largest one.

label: Perspective And Slices
notes: Use this slide to connect epigraphs with two recurring constructions. Horizontal slices explain why sublevel sets of convex functions are convex. When a function is positively homogeneous, its epigraph stretches from the origin like a cone, and the convexity condition can be read as subadditivity. These are the first hints of support and gauge functions later in the course.

label: Strict Versus Non-strict
notes: Draw a clear line between convexity and strict convexity. Convexity allows equality on chords, which is why affine functions and absolute value pieces are still convex. Strict convexity asks the graph to fall below every nontrivial chord. It is useful for uniqueness later, but it is not part of the basic epigraph definition.

label: Strong Convexity
notes: Offer strong convexity as an intuition extension, not as a requirement for the section. Ordinary convexity lets flat regions survive. Strong convexity demands a uniform quadratic amount of bending. The picture should help students remember that a Hessian lower bound is a curvature margin, while the epigraph still supplies the underlying convexity language.

label: Sublevel Warning
notes: This is the important misconception slide. Convex functions always have convex sublevel sets, but that condition alone is weaker than convexity. The cubic example has half-line sublevel sets, yet its chord test can fail. This teaches students not to replace the epigraph or Jensen test with a one-way consequence.

label: Numerical Checks
notes: Translate the lecture into checks that students can run. Chord residuals are the simplest numerical diagnostic. Domain checks catch hidden plus infinity behavior. Hessian checks are useful for smooth examples. The important limitation is that finite sampling can find counterexamples but cannot certify every point unless paired with symbolic or structural reasoning.

label: Failure Gallery
notes: Use the gallery as a debugging checklist. A concave cap fails the chord test. A nonconvex domain fails before values matter. A sublevel-only argument can be too weak. Infinite arithmetic can make a written proof meaningless. Each failure tells students which part of the epigraph or Jensen certificate needs repair.

label: Recap
notes: Close by turning the lecture into a habit. First lift the function to its epigraph. Then test convexity with segments, chords, Jensen mixtures, or curvature certificates. Finally audit the consequences: domains, sublevel sets, strictness, and finite residuals. This routine prepares the next section on operations with convex functions.
